title: The Gracchi: when politics turned violent

predict.q: In 133 BC a tribune's land law was blocked by another tribune's veto. Step on through the year: how do you think the stand-off ended?
options: A compromise worked out in the Senate
A vote that removed the blocker, then a killing
predict.reveal: Tiberius Gracchus had the assembly vote the blocking tribune out of office, then stood again; senators and their supporters beat him to death. Most people expect a compromise: Roman writers called it the first political quarrel in the city to end in killing since the kings.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each side breaking one more unwritten rule when you step on through the years from 133 to 121 BC.
interactive.title: Twelve years, step by step
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A timeline of documented events. At each step you see what happened, and which unwritten rule, if any, someone broke. An unwritten rule here is a custom Romans had long kept although no law required it, such as never removing a tribune from office.
interactive.ignores: What drove the brothers and the senators, which ancient writers tell very differently, and the many other people involved.

numbers.label: The Senate's emergency decree; Gaius dies

explain.text:
Step from the land law to the killing and each move goes one rule further than the last.

Tiberius Gracchus, a tribune, wanted public land shared out among poor citizens. A fellow tribune vetoed the law. Instead of giving way, Tiberius had the assembly vote that tribune out of office, which no one had done before. Then he stood for a second year in a row. Senators feared he was making himself too powerful, and they and their supporters beat him to death.

Ten years later his brother Gaius pushed further reforms. In 121 BC the Senate passed an [[emergency decree]] telling a consul to defend the state, and Gaius and many of his followers were killed.

Nothing in Rome's written laws had changed. What broke were its [[unwritten rules]]: customs everyone had kept. **Once force had settled one quarrel, it could settle the next.**

analogy.text: Like a club whose members always settled rows by a show of hands, until one row ends in a fight and the fighters win.
analogy.breaks: A club can call in outsiders to restore order. Rome had no one above the quarrel to enforce its customs.

say.prompt: In your own words: how did the time of the Gracchi change the way Romans settled political quarrels?
rubric: Both sides broke customs that had kept quarrels peaceful
Opponents killed the reformers instead of out-voting them
After that, force became a way to win political fights
say.model: Tiberius and Gaius pushed their reforms by breaking old customs, like voting out a tribune who blocked them. Their opponents answered by killing them and their supporters. Once violence had settled a quarrel in Rome, later politicians could use it too.

checks.q: Put these events of 133 BC in the order they happened.
items: Tiberius proposes sharing out public land
The assembly votes the blocker out of office
Tiberius is killed by senators and their supporters
checks.why: The veto came first; Tiberius answered it by having the blocker removed, and his opponents answered that with violence.

checks.q: Why did the killing of Tiberius Gracchus matter so much for later Roman politics?
options: It showed force could settle a political quarrel
It ended land reform in Rome for good
It gave tribunes the power to veto the Senate

misconception.1: Land reform carried on: land was still handed out after his death, and his brother Gaius revived the reforms ten years later.
misconception.2: Tribunes already had their veto; this quarrel began with one tribune vetoing another.

checks.why: Political violence in the city had been almost unknown. Once it had worked, later leaders could reach for it too.
